title: trataka
hook: the candle is blown out and the room goes dark: what is a steady gaze for, after that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka moved onto the body: the Gita's gaze at the tip of the nose and between the brows. Somewhere with nothing to look at, did the eyes stop roaming? Day one thousand thirty-two.

What is a steady gaze for, once the candle is out? The sit is over. Someone leans forward and blows. A thread of smoke, the smell of wax, and the room goes dark. Then the light switch, the kitchen, the phone, the street, a crowd of things asking to be looked at. It would be easy to think the practice ended with the flame. Today, the last day of trataka, the Gita suggests where the gaze is meant to end up, and it isn't on a candle at all.
screen: `THE SIT IS OVER. THE FLAME IS OUT.` → `A CROWD OF THINGS ASKS TO BE SEEN.` → `WHERE IS THE GAZE MEANT TO END UP?`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, after the seat, the straight back, the lamp in a windless place, Krishna describes the one whose mind has become steady in yoga. In paraphrase: such a person sees the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self, and sees the same everywhere. The Sanskrit is sama-darshana: same-seeing, an even gaze. Then, in the next verse, Krishna makes it personal. Whoever sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me, I am not lost to them, and they are not lost to me. So the steady gaze isn't the end. It's a training for a different kind of seeing. On a flame, the eyes learn to stop jumping. Here, the steadiness goes out into the world. The same evenness looks at a stranger, a sister, a sparrow, someone difficult, and doesn't swing from wanting to pushing away. Two verses later, Krishna gives that evenness a heart. In paraphrase: the one who, by the measure of one's own self, sees pleasure or pain in every being as the same, that yogi is held to be the highest. Shankara reads it plainly: as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to every being. An even gaze, then, isn't a cold one. Now the road of these seven days, in one breath: a small mark, a windless lamp, eyes turned around, a mind tied to one place, a gaze that is met, a point carried on the body, and today, a gaze that stops picking favorites. One small point, and then everything. In this arc, the flame was never the goal. It was a place for the eyes to learn to be still, so they could look at the world with the same calm.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL, ALL IN THE SELF.` · `SAMA-DARSHANA: AN EVEN GAZE.` · `I AM NOT LOST TO THEM.` · `SEVEN DAYS: FROM A MARK TO THE WORLD.` · then, large: `ONE SMALL POINT, THEN EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Begin with one small point, a flame or a mark, at eye level. Rest the gaze there for a little while, blinking when you need to. Then, slowly, let the gaze soften and widen, without moving the eyes, until it takes in the whole room: the wall, the floor, the light, whatever is there. Try to look at all of it with the same calm you gave the point. No favorites. If the mind starts sorting, liking this, disliking that, come back to the point, then widen again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, practiced, the Gita suggests, until the eyes can rest on everything with the same calm.
Your line: trataka. Today, choose one person you usually look past or look at with a frown, and give them, just once, the same steady look you gave the flame. Day one thousand thirty-two.

howItsDone: Some teachers of meditation in Hindu traditions present single-pointed gazing as a beginning, with the Gita's ideal of seeing the same Self in all beings as where the steadiness leads.

fork.setup: your mind is steady in yoga, the Gita says. how do you now look at the world?
options: at nothing; the eyes stay closed.
fork.reveal: the Gita describes the one steady in yoga as seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, the same everywhere.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sama-darshana, same-seeing, an even gaze. In the Gita, the one steady in yoga sees the same everywhere.

trapdoor: what you thought: trataka is about the candle.
what it means: the candle trains the eyes for an even gaze on the whole world.
what a scholar hears: Gita 6.29, sarvatra sama-darśanaḥ, and 6.30, tasyāhaṃ na praṇaśyāmi.
